name: Freya Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Freya, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Does that sound all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Totally fine. I talk about this stuff constantly, so you might have to stop me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior at Ledgerlight, a twelve-person firm that does the books, year-end accounts and tax for charities, small social enterprises and a few startups. I use AI tools all day: I have one reading bank feeds, one drafting the notes to the accounts, and I check what they spit out. My weak spot is the technical rules, like VAT on mixed charity income, and Joss, one of the founders, says I move fast and check too little, which is fair. The best bit is when a tiny food bank finally understands its own numbers because I made them a one-page summary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. That would be a bit embarrassing for me, since I'm the office's AI enthusiast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, it's a good tool, not a miracle, and I'd probably post a slightly sheepish thread about what actually worked. At work I'd say we should stop paying for the subscriptions that don't earn their keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think a plateau suits me fine, because the routine tasks AI takes off my plate are the dullest ones. I'm already the person who knows how to set it up. My job would get a bit easier, not smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools and get properly good at the dull technical stuff, starting with the VAT course Joss keeps sending me. I'd keep putting money into my index fund every month, like I have since my first job. And I'd write up our prompts properly, so the whole office uses them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly let down, maybe, because I like a big change, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd write up the prompts for the office. What does that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A shared document with the twenty prompts I use, what each one is good and bad at, and a checklist for checking the output. I did a rough version last month and Joss used it for a client report. That's the most useful thing I've done there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything else in your life a worry right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent goes up every year, and I share a house with two friends, which I'm a bit old for. But I've got about ten months saved, so it's more annoying than scary.

say: I'd call AI a **good tool**, not a miracle, in a slightly **sheepish** post.
I'd tell the office to cancel **subscriptions** that don't earn their keep.
think: A **plateau** suits me, because AI takes my **dullest tasks**.
My job would get **easier**, not smaller, since I set the tools up.
do: Take the **VAT course** my boss keeps sending me.
Keep paying into my **index fund** every month.
Write up the office's **twenty prompts** with a checking list.
feel: **Calm**, and slightly let down because I enjoy **big change**.
S0.quote: A plateau suits me fine, because the routine tasks AI takes off my plate are the dullest ones.
fieldNote: She is secure: **ten months** saved, no dependants, and she is the firm's **AI person**.
Her weakness is **technical rules**, which she treats as homework rather than a threat.
She frames even a plateau as a chance to make the office **share tools**.

steps.text: Write a shared guide to the office's twenty AI prompts
Finish the VAT course on charity income
Keep monthly payments into the index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one I think is actually happening. We're halfway there at Ledgerlight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's exciting and it needs managing properly: the gains should go into shorter hours and better pay, not just partner profits. I'd post about a four-day week for accountants. At work I'd say Ledgerlight should become a worker co-op, which I sort of say already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm fine for now, because I'm the one running the tools. But I'm a junior who's below average on the technical side, so if the tools get good at technical rules too, my edge shrinks. And I worry about Sam, our bookkeeper, who's fifty-three and hates all of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd automate as much of the bookkeeping as I can in the first six months, and then push Joss to use the freed time for advice the charities can't afford now. I'd get the office to join the accountants' union branch together. I'd also sit with Sam every Friday afternoon and teach her the tools, slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in an energised way. I'm not scared for me, I'm watching the people around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sam if her job shrank?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, honestly, the data entry bit is going and I'm sorry. Then I'd say her twenty years of knowing which charity treasurers lie about petty cash is the bit that isn't. Sam would roll her eyes at me, but she'd come on Fridays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You want to automate faster while worrying about colleagues. Is that a contradiction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. But if I don't automate the bookkeeping, my boss will buy some software that does it worse and lets our bookkeeper go anyway. I'd rather be in the room deciding how it's done.

say: I'd say gains should fund a **four-day week**, not just partner profits.
I'd keep pushing for the firm to become a **worker co-op**.
think: I'm fine **for now** because I run the tools, but my edge could **shrink**.
I worry most about our **fifty-three-year-old** bookkeeper, who hates the tools.
do: **Automate** most of the bookkeeping within **six months**.
Get the office to join the **union branch** together.
Teach our bookkeeper the tools every **Friday afternoon**.
feel: **Uneasy** but energised, watching **colleagues** more than myself.
S1.quote: If I don't automate the bookkeeping, my boss will buy some software that does it worse and lets our bookkeeper go anyway.
fieldNote: Her own **job** looks safe because she owns the **tools**, which keeps her at uneasy.
She openly holds a **contradiction**: automating fast while defending a colleague.
Progressive instincts show up as a **co-op** and **union** push, not resistance to tech.

steps.text: Automate most of the charity bookkeeping within six months
Get the whole office to join the accountants' union branch
Teach the bookkeeper the AI tools every Friday afternoon

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that's different. That's not tools, that's replacement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a public response immediately: an income guarantee, public ownership of some of these systems, rules on layoffs. I'd be posting every day and I'd be at every meeting. At work I'd say we should decide together how Ledgerlight handles it, before Joss decides alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job goes, and fast. If AI does all thinking work by 2028, being good at prompts is worth nothing, because the AI writes its own prompts. The only good news is I'm twenty-seven with no kids and a year's money, so I'm the one who can take a hit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first months helping small charities set the systems up for free or cheap, because they'll get forgotten otherwise, and I'd do that as paid freelance work on the side. I'd join a group campaigning for an income guarantee. And I'd start looking at work that's about people in a room: organising, community work, maybe running a food co-op.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frozen. It's a bit like being told the house is on fire while you're already holding the fire extinguisher.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're the one who can take a hit. What would you lose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job, my savings slowly, maybe the chance to buy anywhere for years. But nobody depends on me. My mum depends on her pension and my brother has two kids, so I'd rather the hit landed on me than on them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your brother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my brother to stop his kids' savings going into anything tied to office jobs. Then I'd offer to help with childcare if he loses hours. That's what family's for.

say: I'd demand an **income guarantee**, public ownership and **layoff rules** immediately.
I'd push colleagues to decide **together**, before the founder decides alone.
think: My job **goes fast**, and prompt skills become **worthless** at full AGI.
I'm twenty-seven with no kids and a year saved, so I can **take a hit**.
do: Help small charities set up systems as **paid freelance** side work.
Join a campaign for an **income guarantee**.
Look at **people-facing work** like organising or a food co-op.
feel: **Anxious** but not frozen, already holding the **fire extinguisher**.
S2.quote: If AI does all thinking work by 2028, being good at prompts is worth nothing, because the AI writes its own prompts.
fieldNote: She **expects to lose** her job but feels real **control**, so anxious rather than alarmed.
Her cushion and lack of **dependants** make her willing to absorb the shock.
She turns quickly to **people work** and community, true to her progressive outlook.

steps.text: Set up AI systems for small charities as paid freelance work
Join a campaign for a national income guarantee
Apply for community organising or food co-op jobs
Get colleagues to agree a joint plan before the founder acts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay. That's enough time to do something deliberate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years to build the safety net, and I'd say it with a lot of graphs. I'd want the accountants' union to bargain for retraining funds now, while firms are still making money from people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I get two or three good years of being the AI person, and then the AI person isn't needed either. Five years means I can qualify, save hard and move into something else on purpose rather than in a scramble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify in the next eighteen months, because it opens doors to charity finance director roles in the short term. I'd put an extra three hundred a month into the index fund. Around 2029 I'd retrain in community development, part-time, and maybe co-found a small co-op that does finance for charities using AI, owned by the people who work there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, but focused. Five years is a to-do list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still want to buy a home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not until it settles. I'd rather keep my money liquid than lock it into a mortgage on a salary that might vanish. My parents think that's mad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame, if anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the technology. I'd blame a system where the gains go to whoever owns the servers. If the people doing the work owned a share of the servers, nobody would be this frightened of AI.

say: I'd say there are **five years** to build the **safety net**.
I'd want the union to bargain for **retraining funds** now.
think: I get two or three years as the **AI person**, then that's not needed either.
Five years lets me move **on purpose**, not in a **scramble**.
do: Qualify within **eighteen months** for charity finance roles.
Put an extra **three hundred** a month into the index fund.
feel: **Anxious** but focused, treating five years as a **to-do list**.
S3.quote: If the people doing the work owned a share of the servers, nobody would be this frightened of AI.
fieldNote: She blames **ownership**, not the technology, a clear progressive frame.
She keeps money **liquid** rather than buying a home, against her parents' advice.
Even the AI-savvy role she holds has a short **shelf life** in her own view.

steps.text: Qualify within eighteen months to reach charity finance roles
Add three hundred a month to the index fund
Keep savings in cash instead of buying a home
Push the union to bargain for retraining funds now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's long enough to actually build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it, and a disaster if we don't. I'd post about it, I'd go to the union, and I'd probably bore my flatmates to death about it over dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think by 2036 I won't be doing accounts, but I might be running something that uses AI to do them, owned with other people. That feels more like a door than a wall. Robots being three years later doesn't matter for me, because almost none of my job is hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify, work at Ledgerlight a few more years, and keep building the charity side work. By about 2030 I'd want to co-found the co-op properly, putting in maybe ten thousand of my savings. I'd keep up the campaigning too, because a co-op doesn't help the bookkeepers who never get the chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly uneasy. Excited, really, with a worry underneath about everyone who doesn't have my options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the co-op fails?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I've lost ten thousand and I'm thirty-something with a lot of experience setting up AI systems. I'd survive. My dad lost his shop in his forties and he survived, though it took him years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell younger people to go into accounting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'd tell my little cousin to learn how organisations work and how to talk to people, and to learn the AI as a tool, not a career. Accounting as a job title probably won't mean much by then.

say: I'd call ten years a **gift** if used and a **disaster** if not.
I'd keep campaigning so **bookkeepers** without options aren't left behind.
think: By **2036** I may run a firm that uses AI to do accounts, **co-owned**.
The **robot delay** doesn't help me, since my job has almost **no hands-on** work.
do: Put about **ten thousand** of savings into co-founding a **co-op** by 2030.
Grow the **charity side work** while still at the firm.
Keep **campaigning** through the union for those left behind.
feel: Mostly **uneasy**, excited, with worry for people **without options**.
S4.quote: By 2036 I won't be doing accounts, but I might be running something that uses AI to do them, owned with other people.
fieldNote: She sees the decade as a **door**, which with her savings keeps her at uneasy.
She accepts a real **risk** to savings, citing her father surviving a **lost shop**.
Her worry is mostly for **others**, which shapes her campaigning.

steps.text: Put about ten thousand of savings into co-founding an accounting co-op
Grow paid AI set-up work for charities alongside the job
Campaign through the union for retraining for bookkeepers

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, but not really for me. It worries me for Sam, for my brother, for everyone who can't move fast. What would help is an income guarantee that starts before the layoffs, not after, and some public ownership of these systems.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns it. Everyone asks whether AI will take jobs, but nobody asks who gets the money when it does.

headlineQuote: Everyone asks whether AI will take jobs, but nobody asks who gets the money when it does.
portrait: Freya is a **junior accountant** at a twelve-person firm serving charities and startups, and its everyday **AI user**.
She is weak on **technical rules** but strong on tools, with ten months saved and no dependants.
She stays calm to uneasy in milder worlds, and **anxious** when AGI arrives soon.
She blames **ownership**, not technology, and pushes for a union, a co-op and an **income guarantee**.
Her plan is to co-found a **worker-owned** finance co-op for charities.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028**, mainly for colleagues and family who can't **move fast**.
whatWouldHelp: An **income guarantee** that starts before layoffs, and some **public ownership** of AI systems.
